analysis.one_liner: Forces ticket sellers and resellers to disclose fees, ticket counts, and seat details, and blocks resellers from hoarding new tickets for 48 hours.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee: no hearings, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules for selling and reselling tickets to concerts, sports, and other events. Primary sellers would have to publish how many tickets exist and how many are set aside before the public sale, show all fees in the advertised price, and refund those fees. Resellers would have to register with the FTC, disclose the ticket's face value and exact seat, say whether they actually hold the ticket, and wait 48 hours after a ticket goes on public sale before buying it to resell. Online resale marketplaces would have to warn buyers clearly and reveal when the seller is the venue, artist, or primary ticketing company itself. The bill was referred to a House committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy tickets to concerts, sports, and other live events would gain: they would see the true total price with all fees before buying, learn how many tickets actually exist and how many are held back, and see a resold ticket's face value and exact seat before paying a markup. The 48-hour cooling-off period would give ordinary fans a window to buy hot tickets before professional resellers do.

how_it_helps.text: Primary sellers would have to disclose, at least a week before a sale, how many tickets exist and how many are held back for pre-sales, giveaways, or insiders — letting buyers know what is actually available to them.

All service, convenience, and parking fees would have to be shown with the ticket price in advertising and printed on the ticket, and included in refunds, ending the practice of quoting a low base price and adding fees at checkout.

Resellers would have to disclose the ticket's face value and seat location, say whether they actually possess the ticket, and online marketplaces would have to tell buyers when the seller is the venue, artist, or primary ticketer itself.
Resellers would be barred from buying tickets during the first 48 hours of public sale, targeting the practice of using automated purchasing to grab the best seats before fans can.
Violations would be enforced by the FTC as deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents for refunds, damages, and penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Primary ticket sellers, venues, and professional resellers would bear the cost: publishing ticket inventories and holdbacks, itemizing fees, registering with the FTC, and losing the ability to buy up tickets in the first 48 hours. Online marketplaces like resale sites would face registration, disclosure, and enforcement exposure, and would lose sales that rest on buyers not knowing a seller is the venue or artist itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ticket resellers, marketplaces, and primary sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill depended on the FTC writing detailed rules within 180 days, so the actual strength of protections — and the burden on sellers — would be decided by regulators rather than by Congress, and rulemaking could delay or soften the requirements.

Some requirements would add compliance costs for sellers and marketplaces (registration, pre-sale disclosures, printing distribution methods on tickets), costs that could be passed to consumers in ticket prices; the 48-hour resale ban also limits a legal market, including for season-ticket holders reselling games they cannot attend — though the bill exempts season tickets and bundled series.

The bill exempts individuals reselling fewer than 25 tickets a year, so casual resellers — including some operating as small-scale brokers — would remain outside the registration and disclosure system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to concert and sports fans are real but the design has some rough edges. The strong parts are the anti-speculation rule (no buying tickets in the first 48 hours), the mandate to show full prices with all fees, and letting state attorneys general sue. The weaker parts are the reliance on FTC rulemaking (which can dilute requirements), the exemption for anyone reselling fewer than 25 tickets a year, and a 48-hour bar that season-ticket holders and bundled packages escape. On balance it would have shifted information power back to buyers at modest cost to sellers, and it died before anyone could weigh the tradeoffs in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then a subcommittee two days later, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bill Pascrell introduced the bill on June 2, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day, June 3, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill's support was modest: 17 House Democrats cosponsored it, with no Republican cosponsors recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Professional ticket resellers, online resale marketplaces, and primary sellers came out ahead: none of the disclosure, registration, or anti-hoarding rules took effect, and fans kept facing hidden fees and seats snapped up within minutes of going on sale.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ticket resellers and marketplaces; fans kept paying

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or reported it out, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection
against.what_they_did: Took jurisdiction of the bill one day after introduction and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split is recorded; its support was entirely Democratic (17 Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans), but the absence of a vote means no one had to take a position.

industries.industry: Online ticket resale marketplaces and professional brokers
industries.note: The bill would force registration with the FTC, disclosure of face value and seat locations, and a ban on buying tickets in the first 48 hours of sale — rules aimed at the core of how large-scale resale operates. Industry interest runs against the buyers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Primary ticket sellers, venues, and promoters
industries.note: They would have to reveal how many tickets exist, how many are withheld from public sale, and all fees up front, and their own employees could not resell above face value. Their interest in hiding holdbacks and fees runs against consumers.
Not a concentrated industry, but the bill's entire purpose is to shift information and pricing power to fans buying tickets. Because the bill died, fans got none of these protections.
